quote: Rewrite the item to the review's actual result, e.g. stem: 'A 2022 Cochrane review of 15 RCTs evaluated Shared Decision-Making (SDM) interventions in mental health care. Which outcome showed some evidence of improvement?' keyed to 'Patients' perceived involvement in the decision-making process immediately after the encounter', with feedback that effects on knowledge, overall satisfaction, and clinical outcomes were uncertain (low- to very-low-certainty evidence). Align Q6's feedback with the same summary, and attribute knowledge/decisional-conflict gains to the general patient decision-aid literature if that teaching point is kept.
problem: The prior review's remediation instruction (A3C2-F007 'replacement') was pasted verbatim into the learner-facing stem; the options, key and feedback were never rewritten, so the item still keys 'Patient satisfaction and knowledge' while its own stem says that finding is uncertain.
whyItMatters: Learners see an editorial instruction instead of a question and a key that contradicts it; the item teaches the Cochrane review backwards.
evidence: Aoki Y et al., Shared decision-making interventions for people with mental health conditions, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;11:CD007297 (doi:10.1002/14651858.CD007297.pub3): 15 RCTs; SDM 'may improve SDM-specific user-reported outcomes from encounters immediately after intervention' (SMD 0.63, low certainty); 'We are uncertain if SDM interventions improve users' overall satisfaction'; 'uncertain whether SDM interventions improve knowledge ... and the relationship between users and healthcare professionals'; clinical outcomes uncertain (very low certainty).
correction: A 2022 Cochrane review of 15 RCTs evaluated shared decision-making (SDM) interventions in mental health care. Which outcome showed some evidence of improvement?
verified: PubMed abstract of Aoki 2022 (PMID 36367232); prior_findings A3C2-F007

quote: Patient satisfaction and knowledge
problem: The keyed answer is the one outcome set the named Cochrane review explicitly called uncertain; the only improved outcome was patients' perceived involvement immediately after the encounter (low-certainty evidence).
whyItMatters: Learners and residents would cite the Cochrane review as showing SDM improves knowledge and satisfaction, which it does not.
evidence: Aoki Y et al., Shared decision-making interventions for people with mental health conditions, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;11:CD007297 (doi:10.1002/14651858.CD007297.pub3): 15 RCTs; SDM 'may improve SDM-specific user-reported outcomes from encounters immediately after intervention' (SMD 0.63, low certainty); 'We are uncertain if SDM interventions improve users' overall satisfaction'; 'uncertain whether SDM interventions improve knowledge ... and the relationship between users and healthcare professionals'; clinical outcomes uncertain (very low certainty).
correction: Patients' perceived involvement in the decision immediately after the encounter

quote: The meta-analysis found that SDM interventions effectively enhanced how much patients knew about their treatment and how satisfied they were with the process.
problem: Keyed rationale mis-summarises Aoki 2022, which was uncertain whether SDM improves knowledge or overall satisfaction.
whyItMatters: Teaches an efficacy claim the cited review does not support.
evidence: Aoki Y et al., Shared decision-making interventions for people with mental health conditions, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;11:CD007297 (doi:10.1002/14651858.CD007297.pub3): 15 RCTs; SDM 'may improve SDM-specific user-reported outcomes from encounters immediately after intervention' (SMD 0.63, low certainty); 'We are uncertain if SDM interventions improve users' overall satisfaction'; 'uncertain whether SDM interventions improve knowledge ... and the relationship between users and healthcare professionals'; clinical outcomes uncertain (very low certainty).
correction: The review found low-certainty evidence that SDM interventions increase patients' perceived involvement in the decision immediately after the encounter; effects on knowledge, overall satisfaction and clinical outcomes were uncertain (very-low-certainty evidence).

quote: The Cochrane review noted that while satisfaction and engagement improve, the effects on clinical outcomes like symptom remission are less consistent.
problem: The Cochrane review did not find that satisfaction or engagement improve; overall satisfaction, treatment continuation and knowledge were all uncertain. The prior finding asked for this feedback to be aligned and it was not.
whyItMatters: Repeats the same mis-summary of the review as Q2.
evidence: Aoki Y et al., Shared decision-making interventions for people with mental health conditions, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;11:CD007297 (doi:10.1002/14651858.CD007297.pub3): 15 RCTs; SDM 'may improve SDM-specific user-reported outcomes from encounters immediately after intervention' (SMD 0.63, low certainty); 'We are uncertain if SDM interventions improve users' overall satisfaction'; 'uncertain whether SDM interventions improve knowledge ... and the relationship between users and healthcare professionals'; clinical outcomes uncertain (very low certainty).
correction: The Cochrane review found only low-certainty evidence that SDM increases patients' perceived involvement immediately after the encounter; effects on satisfaction, engagement and clinical outcomes such as symptom remission were uncertain.

quote: The evidence suggests that SDM actually improves the therapeutic relationship and treatment engagement.
problem: The best available evidence (Aoki 2022) was uncertain whether SDM improves the user-clinician relationship or treatment/medication continuation.
whyItMatters: States as evidence-based a benefit the systematic review could not establish.
evidence: Aoki Y et al., Shared decision-making interventions for people with mental health conditions, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;11:CD007297 (doi:10.1002/14651858.CD007297.pub3): 15 RCTs; SDM 'may improve SDM-specific user-reported outcomes from encounters immediately after intervention' (SMD 0.63, low certainty); 'We are uncertain if SDM interventions improve users' overall satisfaction'; 'uncertain whether SDM interventions improve knowledge ... and the relationship between users and healthcare professionals'; clinical outcomes uncertain (very low certainty).
correction: There is no evidence that SDM harms the therapeutic relationship; its effects on the relationship and on treatment engagement remain uncertain.

quote: Rewrite the item to the trial's published finding, e.g. stem: 'In BALANCE, how did lithium monotherapy compare with valproate monotherapy for relapse prevention?' keyed to 'Lithium was superior at preventing new intervention for an emergent mood episode of either pole (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.51-1.00)', with feedback noting the primary outcome covered relapse of any polarity and the trial did not establish a specific depressive-pole advantage. Do not key a polarity-specific claim or the 0.63 figure unless it is verified against the paper's polarity-specific secondary outcomes in the full report.
problem: The prior remediation instruction (A3C2-F006 'replacement') was pasted in as the keyed feedback, while the stem and key ('Depressive relapses') were left unchanged; the feedback now says the key it explains is unestablished. The 'Manic relapses' and 'Mixed episodes' distractor feedbacks still assert a depressive-pole advantage.
whyItMatters: Learners see an editorial instruction, and the item still teaches an unverified polarity-specific claim for choosing a maintenance agent; the stem/key need rewriting (or the item withdrawn) along the lines the instruction describes.
evidence: Geddes JR et al. (BALANCE), Lancet 2010;375:385-95 (doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(09)61828-6): primary outcome new intervention for an emergent mood episode of either pole; lithium vs valproate HR 0.71 (95% CI 0.51-1.00), combination vs valproate HR 0.59.
correction: BALANCE's primary outcome was new intervention for an emergent mood episode of either pole: lithium monotherapy was superior to valproate monotherapy (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.51–1.00). The published report does not establish that lithium's advantage was specific to depressive relapse.
verified: prior_findings A3C2-F006 verification; recall of BALANCE abstract

quote: The study suggests that the combination of lithium and valproate is appropriate and effective for patients who do not fully respond to one agent.
problem: BALANCE did not study partial responders, and combination therapy was not significantly better than lithium monotherapy (HR ~0.82, CI crossing 1); it was superior only to valproate monotherapy.
whyItMatters: Learners would believe BALANCE showed adding valproate beats lithium alone, when the trial's lesson is that lithium-containing regimens beat valproate alone.
evidence: Geddes JR et al., Lancet 2010 (BALANCE): combination vs valproate HR 0.59 (0.42-0.83); combination vs lithium HR 0.82 (0.57-1.20), not significant.
correction: BALANCE found combination therapy and lithium monotherapy each superior to valproate monotherapy, but combination was not significantly better than lithium alone; adding valproate for partial lithium response is a reasonable clinical option rather than a result BALANCE tested.
verified: recall (combination-vs-lithium HR from the Lancet 2010 report)

quote: In the context of the STEP-BD program, how did the recovery rates in the intensive psychotherapy trial compare to the recovery rates in the antidepressant medication trial?
problem: The prior fix corrected only the keyed option; the stem still asks for a cross-trial comparison that was never made, and the keyed answer (psychotherapy vs collaborative care) no longer answers the question asked.
whyItMatters: Learners infer STEP-BD showed psychotherapy outperforming antidepressants, a comparison that was never randomized.
evidence: Miklowitz DJ et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2007;64:419-26 (doi:10.1001/archpsyc.64.4.419): 1-year recovery 64.4% intensive psychotherapy vs 51.5% collaborative care, all on protocol pharmacotherapy; Sachs GS et al., NEJM 2007: durable recovery 23.5% vs 27.3% over 26 weeks — separate randomization, different outcome and horizon.
correction: In the companion STEP-BD psychosocial trial, how did 1-year recovery with intensive psychotherapy compare with brief collaborative care?

quote: Data from the companion trial showed that psychotherapy (CBT, IPSRT, FFT) was highly effective compared to the medication-only outcomes.
problem: There were no 'medication-only outcomes': both psychosocial arms received protocol pharmacotherapy, and the comparator was brief collaborative care.
whyItMatters: Teaches a psychotherapy-vs-medication comparison STEP-BD never tested.
evidence: Miklowitz DJ et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2007;64:419-26 (doi:10.1001/archpsyc.64.4.419): 1-year recovery 64.4% intensive psychotherapy vs 51.5% collaborative care, all on protocol pharmacotherapy; Sachs GS et al., NEJM 2007: durable recovery 23.5% vs 27.3% over 26 weeks — separate randomization, different outcome and horizon.
correction: In the companion trial, intensive psychotherapy (CBT, IPSRT or FFT) added to mood-stabilizer pharmacotherapy produced higher 1-year recovery (64%) than brief collaborative care (52%); it was never compared head-to-head with the antidepressant trial.

quote: The psychotherapy trial showed significantly higher rates of recovery compared to the medication-focused trial.
problem: Asserts a statistical comparison between two separately randomized trials with different outcome definitions (durable recovery at 26 weeks vs recovery within 1 year).
whyItMatters: Learners would quote a significance test that does not exist.
evidence: Miklowitz DJ et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 2007;64:419-26 (doi:10.1001/archpsyc.64.4.419): 1-year recovery 64.4% intensive psychotherapy vs 51.5% collaborative care, all on protocol pharmacotherapy; Sachs GS et al., NEJM 2007: durable recovery 23.5% vs 27.3% over 26 weeks — separate randomization, different outcome and horizon.
correction: The two trials were separate randomizations with different outcome definitions and timeframes, so their recovery rates cannot be compared statistically.

quote: The 2024 paper by Kirkbride et al. in 'World Psychiatry' used which of the following methods to establish the evidence base for social determinants of mental health?
problem: Misattribution: the 'umbrella review of 26 meta-analyses' (keyed) and the food-insecurity medium-effect finding (Q2) belong to Alon et al., Psychiatry Research 2024, not Kirkbride et al., World Psychiatry 2024, which is a narrative roadmap review.
whyItMatters: Learners (and residents citing it) attach the wrong method and findings to a landmark paper; anyone checking Kirkbride will not find the keyed content.
evidence: Alon N, ... Jeste DV. Social determinants of mental health in major depressive disorder: umbrella review of 26 meta-analyses and systematic reviews. Psychiatry Res 2024;335:115854 (doi:10.1016/j.psychres.2024.115854): childhood abuse/neglect, IPV in females and food insecurity associated with MDD with medium effect sizes. Kirkbride JB et al., World Psychiatry 2024;23:58-90 (doi:10.1002/wps.21160) is a narrative evidence-and-prevention roadmap across disorders, not a 26-meta-analysis umbrella review.
correction: The 2024 umbrella review by Alon et al. in 'Psychiatry Research' used which of the following methods to establish the evidence base for social determinants of major depressive disorder?

quote: Caffeine intake is not among the key social determinants discussed in the Kirkbride review of MDD risk.
problem: Same misattribution: the MDD-specific umbrella review is Alon et al. 2024.
whyItMatters: Perpetuates the wrong citation for the food-insecurity finding.
evidence: Alon N, ... Jeste DV. Social determinants of mental health in major depressive disorder: umbrella review of 26 meta-analyses and systematic reviews. Psychiatry Res 2024;335:115854 (doi:10.1016/j.psychres.2024.115854): childhood abuse/neglect, IPV in females and food insecurity associated with MDD with medium effect sizes. Kirkbride JB et al., World Psychiatry 2024;23:58-90 (doi:10.1002/wps.21160) is a narrative evidence-and-prevention roadmap across disorders, not a 26-meta-analysis umbrella review.
correction: Caffeine intake is not among the social determinants examined in the Alon et al. umbrella review of MDD risk.

quote: The study found an MMSE decline of −2.4 points over 36 weeks in the antipsychotic group compared to placebo, representing significant acceleration of the disease process.
problem: The −2.4-point MMSE figure is the overall decline across all CATIE-AD patients (drug and placebo) over 36 weeks, not the antipsychotic-minus-placebo difference.
whyItMatters: Learners would quote a drug effect roughly an order of magnitude too large as the CATIE-AD cognitive harm.
evidence: Vigen CL et al., Am J Psychiatry 2011;168:831-9 (doi:10.1176/appi.ajp.2011.08121844): 'Overall, patients showed steady, significant declines ... MMSE; -2.4 points over 36 weeks'; cognition declined more with antipsychotics than placebo on MMSE, BPRS cognitive subscale and a cognitive summary score, 'consistent with 1 year's deterioration compared with placebo'.
correction: All patients declined (MMSE −2.4 points over 36 weeks overall), and decline was significantly greater with antipsychotics than with placebo on the MMSE, BPRS cognitive subscale and a cognitive summary score — a magnitude the authors equated to about one year's additional deterioration.

quote: The trial specifically identified a −2.4 point difference in MMSE scores, indicating a distinct disadvantage for those on active medication.
problem: Same error: −2.4 is the whole-sample decline, not a between-group difference.
whyItMatters: Reinforces the mis-stated effect size.
evidence: Vigen CL et al., Am J Psychiatry 2011;168:831-9 (doi:10.1176/appi.ajp.2011.08121844): 'Overall, patients showed steady, significant declines ... MMSE; -2.4 points over 36 weeks'; cognition declined more with antipsychotics than placebo on MMSE, BPRS cognitive subscale and a cognitive summary score, 'consistent with 1 year's deterioration compared with placebo'.
correction: The trial found significantly greater cognitive decline with antipsychotics than with placebo on several measures, including the MMSE.

quote: The trial and subsequent meta-analyses confirm that antipsychotics significantly increase the risk of death in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.
problem: CATIE-AD did not test or demonstrate a mortality increase; the boxed warning (2005) predates CATIE-AD (2006) and rests on pooled placebo-controlled trials (FDA analysis; Schneider et al., JAMA 2005, OR ~1.54). The stem's 'corroborated by the CATIE-AD source material' repeats the attribution.
whyItMatters: Learners attribute the mortality signal to the wrong study and overstate what CATIE-AD showed.
evidence: Schneider LS, Dagerman KS, Insel P. JAMA 2005;294:1934-43 (OR 1.54); FDA Public Health Advisory, April 2005; Schneider LS et al., NEJM 2006;355:1525-38 (CATIE-AD primary outcome time to discontinuation).
correction: Pooled placebo-controlled trials (FDA analysis; Schneider et al., JAMA 2005) show antipsychotics increase mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis; CATIE-AD itself was not designed to test mortality.

quote: Combined treatment is superior to either pharmacotherapy or psychotherapy alone.
problem: Mis-keyed: the cited meta-analysis found combined treatment superior to pharmacotherapy alone but NOT more effective than CBT alone at short or long term.
whyItMatters: Learners would state on rounds and exams that the paper showed combination beats psychotherapy, the opposite of its finding.
evidence: Cuijpers P et al., World Psychiatry 2023;22:105-15 (doi:10.1002/wps.21069): 'Combined treatment was more effective than pharmacotherapies alone ... but it was not more effective than CBT alone at either time point'; 'CBT was significantly more effective than other psychotherapies, but the difference was small (g=0.06) and became non-significant in most sensitivity analyses.'
correction: Combined treatment is superior to pharmacotherapy alone but was not significantly more effective than CBT alone.

quote: The meta-analysis confirmed that the synergy of medication and therapy provides better outcomes than either treatment modality used in isolation.
problem: Rationale inverts the finding for CBT alone.
whyItMatters: Same false belief as the key.
evidence: Cuijpers P et al., World Psychiatry 2023;22:105-15 (doi:10.1002/wps.21069): 'Combined treatment was more effective than pharmacotherapies alone ... but it was not more effective than CBT alone at either time point'; 'CBT was significantly more effective than other psychotherapies, but the difference was small (g=0.06) and became non-significant in most sensitivity analyses.'
correction: The meta-analysis found combined treatment more effective than pharmacotherapy alone at short and longer-term follow-up, but not more effective than CBT alone.

quote: The study found combined treatment to be superior to both individual modalities, not just therapy.
problem: Distractor feedback repeats the inverted finding.
whyItMatters: Reinforces the mis-keyed answer.
evidence: Cuijpers P et al., World Psychiatry 2023;22:105-15 (doi:10.1002/wps.21069): 'Combined treatment was more effective than pharmacotherapies alone ... but it was not more effective than CBT alone at either time point'; 'CBT was significantly more effective than other psychotherapies, but the difference was small (g=0.06) and became non-significant in most sensitivity analyses.'
correction: The reverse: combined treatment was superior to pharmacotherapy alone but not to CBT alone.

quote: Observing that combined treatment is more effective than psychotherapy alone.
problem: This option is labelled 'a key finding of the study and not an overstatement', but the meta-analysis found combined treatment was not more effective than CBT alone — so it is itself an overstatement and the item is effectively double-keyed.
whyItMatters: Self-contradicting item that teaches the inverted finding a second time.
evidence: Cuijpers P et al., World Psychiatry 2023;22:105-15 (doi:10.1002/wps.21069): 'Combined treatment was more effective than pharmacotherapies alone ... but it was not more effective than CBT alone at either time point'; 'CBT was significantly more effective than other psychotherapies, but the difference was small (g=0.06) and became non-significant in most sensitivity analyses.'
correction: Observing that combined treatment is more effective than pharmacotherapy alone.

quote: There were no significant differences in efficacy between these structured psychotherapies.
problem: In the primary analysis CBT was statistically significantly (though trivially, g=0.06) more effective than other psychotherapies pooled; the difference lost significance in most sensitivity analyses. The paper did not report separate CBT-vs-IPT or CBT-vs-psychodynamic comparisons as the stem implies.
whyItMatters: Learners misreport the paper's result; the defensible teaching point is 'small and not robust', not 'no significant difference'.
evidence: Cuijpers P et al., World Psychiatry 2023;22:105-15 (doi:10.1002/wps.21069): 'Combined treatment was more effective than pharmacotherapies alone ... but it was not more effective than CBT alone at either time point'; 'CBT was significantly more effective than other psychotherapies, but the difference was small (g=0.06) and became non-significant in most sensitivity analyses.'
correction: CBT's advantage over other psychotherapies was very small (g=0.06) and was not robust across sensitivity analyses.

quote: Explaining that the treatment requires regular intravenous infusions.
problem: Outdated: FDA approved subcutaneous lecanemab (Leqembi Iqlik) autoinjector for maintenance dosing (Aug 2025) and subsequently as an initiation dose (2026), so IV infusion is no longer the only route.
whyItMatters: A clinician counselling a family would give outdated administration information.
evidence: Eisai/Biogen FDA approval announcements: Leqembi Iqlik subcutaneous maintenance dosing, 2025-08-29; subcutaneous initiation dose, 2026 (eisai.com/news/2026/news202640).
correction: Explaining that the treatment requires ongoing regular dosing, by intravenous infusion or subcutaneous injection.

quote: 76% responded to lorazepam, and all non-responders subsequently responded to ECT.
problem: Of the 5 lorazepam non-responders, 4 received ECT and those 4 responded; 'all non-responders' overstates it.
whyItMatters: Small overstatement of ECT certainty attributed to the paper.
evidence: Bush G, Fink M, Petrides G, Dowling F, Francis A. Catatonia. II. Acta Psychiatr Scand 1996;93:137-43 (doi:10.1111/j.1600-0447.1996.tb09815.x): 'In 16 of 21 patients (76%) who received a complete trial of lorazepam ... catatonic signs resolved ... Four patients failing lorazepam responded promptly to ECT.'
correction: 76% responded to lorazepam, and the non-responders who went on to ECT all responded promptly.

quote: the study found response rates between 66−100% depending on the case.
problem: The 66–100% range does not appear in the study, which reported a single rate: 16 of 21 (76%).
whyItMatters: Gives the paper a statistic it does not contain.
evidence: Bush G, Fink M, Petrides G, Dowling F, Francis A. Catatonia. II. Acta Psychiatr Scand 1996;93:137-43 (doi:10.1111/j.1600-0447.1996.tb09815.x): 'In 16 of 21 patients (76%) who received a complete trial of lorazepam ... catatonic signs resolved ... Four patients failing lorazepam responded promptly to ECT.'
correction: the study found 16 of 21 patients (76%) given a complete lorazepam trial responded.
